title: The demonic (16.6–16.20)
hook: the Gita's portrait of the other inheritance sounds uncomfortably modern

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhaya, the divine qualities. Twenty-six of them, starting with fearlessness and purity of heart. Your line was fearlessness, purity. Did you do the thing you'd been avoiding? Today, the other list. Day two hundred fourteen.

Hear the word demonic and you probably picture horns, fire, a horror movie. The Gita's picture is much quieter, and more unsettling. It's a person lying awake at night, running the numbers. I got this today. Tomorrow I'll get that. This is mine, and that will be mine too. I beat that rival, and I'll beat the others. Who is like me? It sounds less like a monster and more like a very busy, very anxious person. Maybe someone we've all been, for an evening or two.
screen: `NOT HORNS AND FIRE.` → `SOMEONE AWAKE, RUNNING THE NUMBERS.` → `WHO IS LIKE ME?`

segments.voice: Verse six: there are two kinds of beings in this world, the divine and the asuric, usually translated demonic. In Hindu stories the asuras are the gods' rivals, powerful and proud. Here the word describes a way of living. Verses seven and eight: such people don't know when to act and when to hold back. They say the world has no truth, no ground, no God, and runs on desire alone. Verse ten: gripped by desire that can never be filled, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance. Then verses twelve to fifteen, the monologue from the hook. Bound by hundreds of hopes, they pile up wealth by any means. This I gained today, this wish I'll fulfill. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, strong and happy. Who else is like me? Even their rituals and their giving, verse seventeen says, are done for show, sacrifice in name only. The Gita's verdict is severe: this road leads downward, again and again. Many teachers, especially modern ones, read this chapter less as a label for other people and more as a mirror, though some classical commentators read it as a portrait of a kind of soul. Every one of us has an evening when the monologue runs. And then verse twenty-one names where it all starts, three gates to hell that destroy the self: kama, desire; krodha, anger; and lobha, greed. Shut those three, the Gita says, and a person begins to walk toward the highest. Notice: the gates aren't beliefs or groups of people. They're three movements inside anyone. That's the word today: the demonic.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF BEINGS.` · `THIS IS MINE. WHO IS LIKE ME?` · `A MIRROR, NOT A LABEL.` · `DESIRE, ANGER, GREED.` · then, large: `THE DEMONIC.`

segments.voice: Sit, and listen for the monologue. Is there a list running? Something to get, someone to beat, something that's mine? Don't argue with it. Just hear it, the way you'd hear a radio in another room. Then check the three gates. Is desire pulling? Is anger simmering? Is there a grasping for more? Wherever one is open, breathe out slowly, and let it close a little. The bell holds the time.
The demonic. Gita sixteen: the asuric way of living, restless, proud and grasping, and the three gates that lead there: desire, anger and greed.
Your line: the three gates of hell. Desire, anger, greed. Today, when you feel one of them swing open, name it, and take one breath before you walk through. Day two hundred fourteen.

screen: `DAY 214 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOLLOW THE SCRIPTURE, NOT DESIRE.`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often read Gita 16 as a mirror for self-examination rather than a way to label others; the three gates of 16.21, kama, krodha and lobha (desire, anger, greed), are widely quoted.

match.prompt: the other inheritance — tap the pairs.
pairs: the gods' proud rivals in the stories

myth: the Gita's 'demonic' person is pictured with horns and fire

the three gates in 16.21 are desire, anger and greed
kama, krodha, lobha: three movements inside anyone.

fork.setup: the Gita names three gates that lead a person down. what are they?
fork.reveal: desire, anger and greed, 16.21. the gates are movements inside a person, not outside threats.

original.note: Sanskrit: asura, in the stories the proud rivals of the devas; Gita 16 uses 'asuri', asuric, for a way of living.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'demonic' means evil beings out there.
what it means: in Gita 16 it's a way of living, restless, proud and grasping, entered through desire, anger and greed.
what a scholar hears: 16.13–16.15 give the asuric monologue ('idam adya maya labdham', this I gained today); 16.21 names the three gates, kama, krodha, lobha.

notes: The carry ('the three gates of hell') is in 16.21, which the outline assigns to day 215; the script teaches it here because the carry requires it, and day 215 builds on it. A Keeper or the owner may want to adjust the outline's verse ranges.
16.19–16.20 (being cast into asuric wombs) is summarized as 'this road leads downward, again and again'; check that this is fair.
'Commentators across schools read this chapter... as a mirror' is a general teaching claim; confirm.

Audit (second sample): the teach credited 'their giving and rituals are for show' to verse 15; the ostentatious sacrifice is 16.17 (16.15 is the boast 'I will sacrifice, I will give'), so it now says verse seventeen. The unsupported 'commentators across schools read it as a mirror' was softened to 'many teachers, especially modern ones', with a note that some classical commentators (e.g. Madhva's school) read the chapter as describing kinds of souls; the matching myth item was changed to fit.
